2.2. Citrus Flavonoids and Lipid Metabolism.
Lipids are essential for maintaining various physiologic and static processes within the body. Dysregulation of the lipid and lipoprotein metabolism is one of the major risk factors leading to CVD, obesity, diabetes, and inflammation. Several studies have demonstrated the beneficial role of citrus flavonoids in modulating lipid metabolism and attenuating several diseases, including obesity and atherosclerosis. However, the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of citrus flavonoids are not fully understood. While human studies have emphasized the dose, bioavailability, efficacy, and safety, citrus flavonoids can improve HDL function via attenuating oxidative stress and inflammation.

Millar et al. have recently discussed the effects of flavonoids on reverse cholesterol transport (RCT), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism, and HDL function.





Previous work from our laboratory showed improved serum HDL levels in type 2 diabetic rats treated with hesperidin and naringin [21]. Long-term consumption of flavonoid-rich foods has been associated with improved circulating levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL-cholesterol [87]. Preclinical in vitro and in vivo studies reported the influence of flavonoids on RCT and HDL function by regulating the activity and expression of hepatic paraoxonase 1 and cholesterol efflux from macrophages [46]. However, clinical studies targeting the effect of citrus flavonoids on HDL function are lacking [46].

ABSTRACT: The active ingredients of Citrus aurantium have been shown to possess a variety of biological activities, especially anti-inflammatory effects. However, its antiatherosclerotic effects need to be further investigated. The aim of this study is to identify compounds with antiatherosclerotic effects from C. aurantium and to further investigate their mechanisms. Three compounds were separated, and then their antiatherosclerotic effect on foam cells induced by oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) was screened by oil red O staining, BODIPY staining, and Dil-ox-LDL uptake measurement. Cholesterol uptake, cholesterol efflux, RT-PCR, and Western blot analysis were used to comprehensively and comparatively explore the potential mechanisms. Nobiletin (NOB), caffeine (CAF), and naringin (NARG), which were separated from C. aurantium, mainly inhibit the formation of foam cells in different ways. NOB reduced cholesterol uptake and enhanced cholesterol efflux and mainly regulated the expressions of ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRA1. CAF promoted cholesterol efflux, mainly by stimulating the expressions of ABCA1 and ABCG1. NARG was more effective in reducing the expression of SRA1 and CD36, which indicated that NARG mainly prevented atherosclerosis by blocking cholesterol uptake. The above results show in detail the antiatherosclerotic activity and mechanism of these compounds, making contributions to their potential applications.

The aim of this study is to identify compounds with antiatherosclerotic effects from C. aurantium and to further investigate their mechanisms. Three compounds were separated, and then their antiatherosclerotic effect on foam cells induced by oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) was screened by oil red O staining, BODIPY staining, and Dil-ox-LDL uptake measurement. Cholesterol uptake, cholesterol efflux, RT-PCR, and Western blot analysis were used to comprehensively and comparatively explore the potential mechanisms. Nobiletin (NOB), caffeine (CAF), and naringin (NARG), which were separated from C. aurantium, mainly inhibit the formation of foam cells in different ways. NOB reduced cholesterol uptake and enhanced cholesterol efflux and mainly regulated the expressions of ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRA1. CAF promoted cholesterol efflux, mainly by stimulating the expressions of ABCA1 and ABCG1. NARG was more effective in reducing the expression of SRA1 and CD36, which indicated that NARG mainly prevented atherosclerosis by blocking cholesterol uptake. The above results show in detail the antiatherosclerotic activity and mechanism of these compounds, making contributions to their potential applications.

Combined with the previous experimental studies, this study compared the antiatherosclerosis effects of NOB, CAF, and NARG isolated from C. aurantium. Under atherogenic conditions, lack of ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRB1 can lead to the reduction of cholesterol efflux, and excessive cholesterol uptake is compelling as CD36 and SRA1 expressions are significantly increased. Therefore, targeting cholesterol efflux and uptake could be an effective strategy to regulate cholesterol metabolism in macrophages and treat atherosclerotic vascular diseases. The results suggested that NOB, CAF, and NARG significantly inhibited foam cell formation. In support, Choe et al. found that NARG displayed great antiatherogenic potential by suppressing the intercellular adhesion molecule-1 in vivo. The protective role of CAF against LDL oxidation was also confirmed. NOB potently reduced atherosclerosis development, as mainly reflected by increased ABCA1 and ABCG1, and decreased SRA1 in ox-LDL-mediated RAW264.7 cells, consistent with their effects on cholesterol uptake and efflux. NARG was more effective in blocking the expressions of SRA1 and CD36 compared with those on ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRB1. In support, an earlier publication was also a strong advocate of the role of NARG in preventing atherosclerosis with a reasonable action mechanism. In contrast, CAF mainly worked by the stimulation of ABCA1 and ABCG1.

# Cytotoxicity in U87 MG cells  
U87 MG, a human Glioblastoma cell line frequently used as a model for cytotoxicity evaluation was adopted in our study for the peptides citrus–amp1 and citrus–amp2. Cells were plated in 96 wells plate (5x10⁴ cells per well), incubated overnight and maintained in a humidified sphere at 37˚C and 5% CO₂. After the incubation period, cells were treated with peptides ranging from 1μM to 128 μM and then incubated for 24h. Untreated and cells treated with DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) were used as positive and negative control for the viability of U87 MG cells. Six replicates were done by each concentration.  
Cytotoxicity was performed using alamarBlue1 cell viability reagent [40], a cell health indicator, through the reduction of viability of living cells. Viable cells convert Resazurin (blue) to Resorufin, a compound that emits red fluorescent light. Alamar Blue medium was prepared by mixing medium with alamarBlue solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a ratio of 10:1. After treatment with the peptides for 24 h, the medium was discarded, and Alamar Blue medium (100 μL) was transferred to a 96-well microplate. The microplates were incubated with Alamar Blue at 37˚C for 4 h, and absorbance was measured using Epoch2 Microplate Reader (Biotek) at 570 nm. Cell viability was calculated using the ratio of the absorbance between treated and untreated cells and the data were expressed as percentages. Three independent experiments were performed.

e) High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (HDLc) and Low-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (LDLc) assay  
High-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) was quantified following the selective precipitation of low-density (LDL) and very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) using a phosphotungstic acid (PTA) and magnesium chloride (MgCl2) reagent. Briefly, 20~mu L of plasma was mixed with 10~mu L of PTA / MgCl2 solution and allowed to stand for 10 minutes before centrifugation at 5,000~rpm for 15 minutes. The resulting supernatant, containing the HDL fraction, was then used for enzymatic cholesterol determination, following the same procedure as for total cholesterol analysis.  
Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) concentrations were calculated using the Friedewald formula.

2.2. Citrus Flavonoids and Lipid Metabolism.
Lipids are essential for maintaining various physiologic and static processes within the body. Dysregulation of the lipid and lipoprotein metabolism is one of the major risk factors leading to CVD, obesity, diabetes, and inflammation. Several studies have demonstrated the beneficial role of citrus flavonoids in modulating lipid metabolism and attenuating several diseases, including obesity and atherosclerosis. However, the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of citrus flavonoids are not fully understood. While human studies have emphasized the dose, bioavailability, efficacy, and safety, citrus flavonoids can improve HDL function via attenuating oxidative stress and inflammation.

Millar et al. have recently discussed the effects of flavonoids on reverse cholesterol transport (RCT), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism, and HDL function.





Previous work from our laboratory showed improved serum HDL levels in type 2 diabetic rats treated with hesperidin and naringin [21]. Long-term consumption of flavonoid-rich foods has been associated with improved circulating levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL-cholesterol [87]. Preclinical in vitro and in vivo studies reported the influence of flavonoids on RCT and HDL function by regulating the activity and expression of hepatic paraoxonase 1 and cholesterol efflux from macrophages [46]. However, clinical studies targeting the effect of citrus flavonoids on HDL function are lacking [46].

4.5. Measurement of Triglyceride, Total Cholesterol and Lipoprotein–Cholesterol Levels in the Plasma.
Blood samples were collected at sacrifice for the isolation of plasma by centrifugation. Plasma concentrations of triglyceride and total cholesterol were measured using enzymatic kits (Randox Laboratories Limited, Crumlin, UK) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A modified phosphotungstic acid/magnesium chloride precipitation procedure was used to isolate low-density lipoprotein and high-density lipoprotein [44]. The concentrations of cholesterol in the high-density lipoprotein-containing supernatants and low-density lipoprotein-containing precipitations were measured using enzymatic kits (Randox Laboratories Limited, Crumlin, UK) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The quantitative standard curve was constructed to determine triglyceride, total cholesterol and lipoprotein–cholesterol levels.

## 2.1 | Synthesis of hexyl gallate  
Hexyl gallate (G6) was synthesized by esterification of gallic acid with n-hexanol as previously described (Silva et al., 2013), with modifications. n-Hexanol (90 mmol, 12 ml) was added to the gallic acid (30 mmol, 5.0 g). The suspension was stirred at 120circ C for 15 min. Catalytic amounts of H2SO4 (3–5 drops) were added to the suspension and stirred at 100circ C. The progress of the reaction was monitored by thin-layer chromatography (TLC). After 5 days, the reaction medium was cooled to room temperature and 50 ml of ethyl acetate added. The residue was partitioned (5 × 50 ml) with 1 M sodium bicarbonate solution and then partitioned with deionized water (5 × 50 ml). The organic fraction was dried under reduced pressure, and this crude product was purified by column chromatography over silica gel using hexane and ethyl acetate (3:2). The structure of hexyl gallate was confirmed by NMR.

2.2. Citrus Flavonoids and Lipid Metabolism.
Lipids are essential for maintaining various physiologic and static processes within the body. Dysregulation of the lipid and lipoprotein metabolism is one of the major risk factors leading to CVD, obesity, diabetes, and inflammation. Several studies have demonstrated the beneficial role of citrus flavonoids in modulating lipid metabolism and attenuating several diseases, including obesity and atherosclerosis. However, the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of citrus flavonoids are not fully understood. While human studies have emphasized the dose, bioavailability, efficacy, and safety, citrus flavonoids can improve HDL function via attenuating oxidative stress and inflammation.

Millar et al. have recently discussed the effects of flavonoids on reverse cholesterol transport (RCT), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism, and HDL function.





Previous work from our laboratory showed improved serum HDL levels in type 2 diabetic rats treated with hesperidin and naringin [21]. Long-term consumption of flavonoid-rich foods has been associated with improved circulating levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL-cholesterol [87]. Preclinical in vitro and in vivo studies reported the influence of flavonoids on RCT and HDL function by regulating the activity and expression of hepatic paraoxonase 1 and cholesterol efflux from macrophages [46]. However, clinical studies targeting the effect of citrus flavonoids on HDL function are lacking [46].

ABSTRACT: The active ingredients of Citrus aurantium have been shown to possess a variety of biological activities, especially anti-inflammatory effects. However, its antiatherosclerotic effects need to be further investigated. The aim of this study is to identify compounds with antiatherosclerotic effects from C. aurantium and to further investigate their mechanisms. Three compounds were separated, and then their antiatherosclerotic effect on foam cells induced by oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) was screened by oil red O staining, BODIPY staining, and Dil-ox-LDL uptake measurement. Cholesterol uptake, cholesterol efflux, RT-PCR, and Western blot analysis were used to comprehensively and comparatively explore the potential mechanisms. Nobiletin (NOB), caffeine (CAF), and naringin (NARG), which were separated from C. aurantium, mainly inhibit the formation of foam cells in different ways. NOB reduced cholesterol uptake and enhanced cholesterol efflux and mainly regulated the expressions of ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRA1. CAF promoted cholesterol efflux, mainly by stimulating the expressions of ABCA1 and ABCG1. NARG was more effective in reducing the expression of SRA1 and CD36, which indicated that NARG mainly prevented atherosclerosis by blocking cholesterol uptake. The above results show in detail the antiatherosclerotic activity and mechanism of these compounds, making contributions to their potential applications.

Combined with the previous experimental studies, this study compared the antiatherosclerosis effects of NOB, CAF, and NARG isolated from C. aurantium. Under atherogenic conditions, lack of ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRB1 can lead to the reduction of cholesterol efflux, and excessive cholesterol uptake is compelling as CD36 and SRA1 expressions are significantly increased. Therefore, targeting cholesterol efflux and uptake could be an effective strategy to regulate cholesterol metabolism in macrophages and treat atherosclerotic vascular diseases. The results suggested that NOB, CAF, and NARG significantly inhibited foam cell formation. In support, Choe et al. found that NARG displayed great antiatherogenic potential by suppressing the intercellular adhesion molecule-1 in vivo. The protective role of CAF against LDL oxidation was also confirmed. NOB potently reduced atherosclerosis development, as mainly reflected by increased ABCA1 and ABCG1, and decreased SRA1 in ox-LDL-mediated RAW264.7 cells, consistent with their effects on cholesterol uptake and efflux. NARG was more effective in blocking the expressions of SRA1 and CD36 compared with those on ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRB1. In support, an earlier publication was also a strong advocate of the role of NARG in preventing atherosclerosis with a reasonable action mechanism. In contrast, CAF mainly worked by the stimulation of ABCA1 and ABCG1.

# Cytotoxicity in U87 MG cells  
U87 MG, a human Glioblastoma cell line frequently used as a model for cytotoxicity evaluation was adopted in our study for the peptides citrus–amp1 and citrus–amp2. Cells were plated in 96 wells plate (5x10⁴ cells per well), incubated overnight and maintained in a humidified sphere at 37˚C and 5% CO₂. Untreated and cells treated with DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) were used as positive and negative control for the viability of U87 MG cells. Six replicates were done by each concentration.  
Cytotoxicity was performed using alamarBlue1 cell viability reagent [40], a cell health indicator, through the reduction of viability of living cells. Viable cells convert Resazurin (blue) to Resorufin, a compound that emits red fluorescent light. Alamar Blue medium was prepared by mixing medium with alamarBlue solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a ratio of 10:1. After treatment with the peptides for 24 h, the medium was discarded, and Alamar Blue medium (100 μL) was transferred to a 96-well microplate. The microplates were incubated with Alamar Blue at 37˚C for 4 h, and absorbance was measured using Epoch2 Microplate Reader (Biotek) at 570 nm. Cell viability was calculated using the ratio of the absorbance between treated and untreated cells and the data were expressed as percentages. Three independent experiments were performed.

2.2. Citrus Flavonoids and Lipid Metabolism.
Lipids are essential for maintaining various physiologic and static processes within the body. Dysregulation of the lipid and lipoprotein metabolism is one of the major risk factors leading to CVD, obesity, diabetes, and inflammation. Several studies have demonstrated the beneficial role of citrus flavonoids in modulating lipid metabolism and attenuating several diseases, including obesity and atherosclerosis. However, the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of citrus flavonoids are not fully understood. While human studies have emphasized the dose, bioavailability, efficacy, and safety, citrus flavonoids can improve HDL function via attenuating oxidative stress and inflammation.

Millar et al. have recently discussed the effects of flavonoids on reverse cholesterol transport (RCT), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism, and HDL function.





Previous work from our laboratory showed improved serum HDL levels in type 2 diabetic rats treated with hesperidin and naringin [21]. Long-term consumption of flavonoid-rich foods has been associated with improved circulating levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL-cholesterol [87]. Preclinical in vitro and in vivo studies reported the influence of flavonoids on RCT and HDL function by regulating the activity and expression of hepatic paraoxonase 1 and cholesterol efflux from macrophages [46]. However, clinical studies targeting the effect of citrus flavonoids on HDL function are lacking [46].

ABSTRACT: The active ingredients of Citrus aurantium have been shown to possess a variety of biological activities, especially anti-inflammatory effects. However, its antiatherosclerotic effects need to be further investigated. The aim of this study is to identify compounds with antiatherosclerotic effects from C. aurantium and to further investigate their mechanisms. Three compounds were separated, and then their antiatherosclerotic effect on foam cells induced by oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) was screened by oil red O staining, BODIPY staining, and Dil-ox-LDL uptake measurement. Cholesterol uptake, cholesterol efflux, RT-PCR, and Western blot analysis were used to comprehensively and comparatively explore the potential mechanisms. Nobiletin (NOB), caffeine (CAF), and naringin (NARG), which were separated from C. aurantium, mainly inhibit the formation of foam cells in different ways. NOB reduced cholesterol uptake and enhanced cholesterol efflux and mainly regulated the expressions of ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRA1. CAF promoted cholesterol efflux, mainly by stimulating the expressions of ABCA1 and ABCG1. NARG was more effective in reducing the expression of SRA1 and CD36, which indicated that NARG mainly prevented atherosclerosis by blocking cholesterol uptake. The above results show in detail the antiatherosclerotic activity and mechanism of these compounds, making contributions to their potential applications.

## Method details  
The goal of the meta-analysis method  
We aim to conduct the meta-analysis examining the variation in vitamin C content based on citrus genotypes and storage conditions, adhering to stringent meta-analytical quality criteria, including selection. The research questions are formulated using the PICO framework, which focuses on the population (P) of experimental units, intervention (I) or treatment, comparison (C) against control, and outcome (O). The meta-analysis separates the factors of storage duration and temperature in relation to the vitamin C content of citrus fruits. Variability that may affect data bias, such as citrus fruit varieties, is minimized by conducting a breakdown at the data analysis stage. The formulation of research questions following the PICO framework is as follows:  
A. Storage Duration Factor  
a. P = How does the duration of storage affect the vitamin C content of citrus fruits?  
b. I = What is the effect of changes in storage duration on vitamin C concentration?  
c. C = How does storage condition on day 0 (post-harvest) compare to longer storage durations in terms of citrus fruit vitamin C concentration?  
d. O = What is the vitamin C concentration after exposure to extended storage duration?  
B. Storage Temperature Factor  
a. P = How do changes in citrus fruit storage temperature affect its vitamin C concentration?  
b. I = What changes in vitamin C result from changes in storage temperature?

2.2. Citrus Flavonoids and Lipid Metabolism.
Lipids are essential for maintaining various physiologic and static processes within the body. Dysregulation of the lipid and lipoprotein metabolism is one of the major risk factors leading to CVD, obesity, diabetes, and inflammation. Several studies have demonstrated the beneficial role of citrus flavonoids in modulating lipid metabolism and attenuating several diseases, including obesity and atherosclerosis. However, the mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of citrus flavonoids are not fully understood. While human studies have emphasized the dose, bioavailability, efficacy, and safety, citrus flavonoids can improve HDL function via attenuating oxidative stress and inflammation.

Millar et al. have recently discussed the effects of flavonoids on reverse cholesterol transport (RCT), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism, and HDL function.





Previous work from our laboratory showed improved serum HDL levels in type 2 diabetic rats treated with hesperidin and naringin [21]. Long-term consumption of flavonoid-rich foods has been associated with improved circulating levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL-cholesterol [87]. Preclinical in vitro and in vivo studies reported the influence of flavonoids on RCT and HDL function by regulating the activity and expression of hepatic paraoxonase 1 and cholesterol efflux from macrophages [46]. However, clinical studies targeting the effect of citrus flavonoids on HDL function are lacking [46].

However, its antiatherosclerotic effects need to be further investigated. NARG was more effective in reducing the expression of SRA1 and CD36, which indicated that NARG mainly prevented atherosclerosis by blocking cholesterol uptake. The above results show in detail the antiatherosclerotic activity and mechanism of these compounds, making contributions to their potential applications.

# Cytotoxicity in U87 MG cells  
U87 MG, a human Glioblastoma cell line frequently used as a model for cytotoxicity evaluation was adopted in our study for the peptides citrus–amp1 and citrus–amp2. Cells were plated in 96 wells plate (5x10⁴ cells per well), incubated overnight and maintained in a humidified sphere at 37˚C and 5% CO₂. After the incubation period, cells were treated with peptides ranging from 1μM to 128 μM and then incubated for 24h. Untreated and cells treated with DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) were used as positive and negative control for the viability of U87 MG cells. Six replicates were done by each concentration.  
Cytotoxicity was performed using alamarBlue1 cell viability reagent [40], a cell health indicator, through the reduction of viability of living cells. Viable cells convert Resazurin (blue) to Resorufin, a compound that emits red fluorescent light. Alamar Blue medium was prepared by mixing medium with alamarBlue solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a ratio of 10:1. After treatment with the peptides for 24 h, the medium was discarded, and Alamar Blue medium (100 μL) was transferred to a 96-well microplate. The microplates were incubated with Alamar Blue at 37˚C for 4 h, and absorbance was measured using Epoch2 Microplate Reader (Biotek) at 570 nm. Cell viability was calculated using the ratio of the absorbance between treated and untreated cells and the data were expressed as percentages. Three independent experiments were performed.

## 3.5. Efflux Inhibition Assay  
The dye efflux assay was executed based on established protocols with slight modifications. Mid-log-phase cultures of E. coli Kam-AcrB, which were grown in MH broth, underwent centrifugation at 5000 x g for 5 min at a temperature of 4circC. Following the centrifugation process, the cells were washed twice with PBS and subsequently diluted in fresh PBS until the OD600 was set to 0.6. After an 8 h incubation at RT, the E. coli cells were exposed to EB at a concentration of 3 mu M for 30 min. The cells were then resuspended twice in PBS buffer and transferred to 96-well plates containing filter-sterilized glucose (25 mM), PAβN (20 mu g/mL ), and various concentrations of apigenin, chrysin, glycitein, and hesperetin at RT, with fluorescence being monitored over a period of 38 min.

Millar et al. have recently discussed the effects of flavonoids on reverse cholesterol transport (RCT), high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism, and HDL function.





Previous work from our laboratory showed improved serum HDL levels in type 2 diabetic rats treated with hesperidin and naringin [21]. Long-term consumption of flavonoid-rich foods has been associated with improved circulating levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, and LDL-cholesterol [87]. Preclinical in vitro and in vivo studies reported the influence of flavonoids on RCT and HDL function by regulating the activity and expression of hepatic paraoxonase 1 and cholesterol efflux from macrophages [46]. However, clinical studies targeting the effect of citrus flavonoids on HDL function are lacking [46].

Combined with the previous experimental studies, this study compared the antiatherosclerosis effects of NOB, CAF, and NARG isolated from C. aurantium. Under atherogenic conditions, lack of ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRB1 can lead to the reduction of cholesterol efflux, and excessive cholesterol uptake is compelling as CD36 and SRA1 expressions are significantly increased. Therefore, targeting cholesterol efflux and uptake could be an effective strategy to regulate cholesterol metabolism in macrophages and treat atherosclerotic vascular diseases. The results suggested that NOB, CAF, and NARG significantly inhibited foam cell formation. In support, Choe et al. found that NARG displayed great antiatherogenic potential by suppressing the intercellular adhesion molecule-1 in vivo. The protective role of CAF against LDL oxidation was also confirmed. NARG was more effective in blocking the expressions of SRA1 and CD36 compared with those on ABCA1, ABCG1, and SRB1. In support, an earlier publication was also a strong advocate of the role of NARG in preventing atherosclerosis with a reasonable action mechanism. # Cytotoxicity in U87 MG cells  
U87 MG, a human Glioblastoma cell line frequently used as a model for cytotoxicity evaluation was adopted in our study for the peptides citrus–amp1 and citrus–amp2. Cells were plated in 96 wells plate (5x10⁴ cells per well), incubated overnight and maintained in a humidified sphere at 37˚C and 5% CO₂. After the incubation period, cells were treated with peptides ranging from 1μM to 128 μM and then incubated for 24h. Untreated and cells treated with DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) were used as positive and negative control for the viability of U87 MG cells. Six replicates were done by each concentration.  
Cytotoxicity was performed using alamarBlue1 cell viability reagent [40], a cell health indicator, through the reduction of viability of living cells. Viable cells convert Resazurin (blue) to Resorufin, a compound that emits red fluorescent light. Alamar Blue medium was prepared by mixing medium with alamarBlue solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in a ratio of 10:1. After treatment with the peptides for 24 h, the medium was discarded, and Alamar Blue medium (100 μL) was transferred to a 96-well microplate. The microplates were incubated with Alamar Blue at 37˚C for 4 h, and absorbance was measured using Epoch2 Microplate Reader (Biotek) at 570 nm. Cell viability was calculated using the ratio of the absorbance between treated and untreated cells and the data were expressed as percentages. Three independent experiments were performed.

Furthermore symbiotic bacteria has been shown to improve larval growth, provide nutritional supplements, which increased fecundity, affect longevity, fix nitrogen and improve sexual performance. In the tephritid fly, symbiotic bacteria have been shown to improve sexual performance, detoxify insecticides and could possibly be a lure for these flies. Understanding the bacteria community structure in different fruit flies will be a first step towards realizing how the roles symbiotic bacteria plays could be exploited in developing an integrated pest management strategy for these flies.  
The Chinese citrus fly Bactrocera minax (Enderlein) is considered unique in the Tephritidae family because of its long over-wintering pupal diapause and its single host, the citrus. B. minax causes huge damage to citrus in China, Nepal, India and Bhutan where it is a major pest. Their overwintering capability with six months of long diapause makes it difficult to manage this pest. So far chemical control has shown to be ineffective probably due to the presence of Gluthinone S-tranferase which plays an important role in detoxification of several insecticides contributing to insecticide resistance in this pest. In addition, commercially available pheromone attractive lures for B. minax males are unavailable. Therefore, there is an urgent need to seek alternative control strategies for their management.

# Assessment of the Bacteria community structure across life stages of the Chinese Citrus Fly, Bactrocera minax (Diptera: Tephritidae)  
## Abstract  
Background: Symbiotic bacteria play a critical role in insect's biology. They also offer great opportunities to improve on current pest management techniques. In order to exploit and integrate the roles played by the gut microbiota on pest management programs, a better understanding of the structural organization of the microbial community in the Chinese citrus fly Bactrocera minax is essential.  
Results: The results revealed a total of 162 OTUs at 97% similarity interval. The dominant bacteria phyla were Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Antinobacteria and Firmicutes, with the Proteobacteria having the highest relative abundance (more than 80% in all life stages). There was also a shift in the dominant OTUs from the early developmental stages to the late developmental stages and adult stages in B. minax. These OTUs related to Klebsiella pneumoniae, Providencia rettgeri and Enterobacter aerogenes, respectively. Six bacteria OTU were shared by all the life stages. These belonged to the Enterobacteriaceae and the Enterococcaceae families.  
Conclusion: The common bacteria groups shared by all the life stages and other fruit flies could be important targets for further research. This should aim towards realizing how these bacteria affect the biology of the fly and how their relationship could be exploited in the development of sustainable management strategies against fruit flies.

## Abstract  
The symbionts, insects, and host plants interlaced in complex relationships. Among them,  insect gut symbionts play an important role in the interactions between insects and host plants. However,  the mechanisms underlying the symbionts involved in the degradation of plant secondary metabolites,  promote insect growth and development, and host adaptation remain largely unclear. As such,  we used the specialist Bactrocera minax as model insect to address this issue. First,  we clarified the effects of gut bacteria in larvae against phenolic secondary metabolites. Through metatranscriptomic  sequencing, we analyzed the composition and abundance of gut symbionts at different life stages of B. minax,  constructed a symbiotic bacteria-mediated phenolic degradation pathway,  and screened two key functional bacteria mediating phenolic degradation. Using in vitro verification and reinfection  experiments,  we elucidated the critical role of larval functional bacteria in adaptation to phenolic compounds. In addition,  the colonization of functional bacteria in B. minax were studied via green fluorescent protein labeling and qPCR  technologies. Finally,  we studied the correlation between gut bacteria of B. minax larvae and the metabolites of different citrus fruits  through 16S rDNA amplicon sequencing and targeted metabolite detection. In fact, insects are multiorganismal symbionts and harbor many microbes that also mediate insecticide resistance (Douglas, 2015). An early study found that Pseudomonas melophthora, an obligate symbiont, helped an insect host (apple maggot, Rhagoletis pomonella) degrade 6 insecticides (Boush and Matsumura, 1967). The densities of symbiotic bacteria Arsenophonus, Rickettsia, and Wolbachia from the Q biotype whitefly associated with the host's susceptibility to thiamethoxam, imidacloprid, pyriproxyfen, and spiromesifen (Ghanim and Kontsedalov, 2009). The symbiotic bacteria Burkholderia mediated the resistance of its insect host, Riptortus pedestris, to the organophosphate pesticide fenitrothion by degrading the pesticide (Kikuchi et al., 2012). Cheng et al. (2017) found that the gut symbiont Citrobacter sp. helps the host insect fruit fly Bactrocera dorsalis degrade the organophosphate insecticide trichlorphon. Pang et al. (2018) found that Arsenophonus strains (S-type Arsenophonus) in the BPH negatively affected the insecticide resistance of the host by downregulating xenobiotic metabolism and increasing amino acid accumulation.

In this study, the majority of the sequence reads belong to Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes and Actinobacteria. B. minax is oligophagous with citrus being its only host plant. Different bacterial species previously described to be associated with citrus plants belong to Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes and Actinobacteria with the Proteobacteria being the most abundant. The host plant is known to have significant effects on insect gut bacteria structure. Symbiotic bacteria of fruit flies have also been reported to be transmitted horizontally and vertically. This suggests that the origin of some of the bacteria found in the gut could be from environmental samples (plant host). Bacteria species which have established unique transmission patterns in fruit flies are those which have co-evolved with the flies. If these bacteria groups could be identified in further studies, they will constitute important target which could be exploited in pest management programs. It is very likely that these bacteria groups could be among the dominant species or core bacteria groups shared by the different life stages.

# Comparative genomic and transcriptomic analyses of chemosensory genes in the citrus fruit fly Bactrocera (Tetradacus) minax
The citrus fruit fly Bactrocera (Tetradacus) minax is a major and devastating agricultural pest in Asian subtropical countries. Previous studies have shown that B. minax interacts with plant hosts via the efficient chemosensory system. However, the molecular components of the B. minax chemosensory system have not been well characterized. Herein, we identified a total of 25 putative odorant-binding receptors (OBPs), 4 single-copy chemosensory proteins (CSPs) and 53 candidate odorant receptors (ORs) using a newly generated whole-genome. minax. This study significantly extended the chemosensation-related gene profiles (particularly, OBPs and ORs) in six other tephritid species. Comparative transcriptome analysis of adult B. minax and Bactrocera dorsalis showed that there were 14 highly expressed OBPs (FPKM > 100) in B. dorsalis and 7 highly expressed ones in B. minax. The expression level of CSP3 gene and CSP4 gene was higher in B. dorsalis than that in B. minax. Comparative genomic and transcriptomic analyses of chemosensory genes in the citrus fruit fly B. minax provided new insights for preventive control of this agriculture important pest and closely related species.

Therefore, this paper takes the citrus fruit fly as the research object and uses insect intestinal microbiota metatrtomics and molecular biology methods to screen the key intestinal symbiotic bacteria that mediate the degradation pathway of phenolic secondary metabolites. From the physiological, biochemical and molecular levels, it systematically explains the mechanism by which the intestinal microbiota of citrus fruit fly larvae assist the host in adapting to plant secondary metabolites.

In addition to the resistance developed by insects themselves to plants, the symbiotes they colonize in the intestinal tract are also related to the resistance metabolism of the host (Dillon and Dillon 2004, Huang et al 2015, Lee et al 2015). Symbiotic microbial communities colonize the intestines of herbivorous insects and interact with the intestinal wall cells of insects and secondary metabolites of plants. They also play a significant role in enhancing the adaptability of insect hosts to toxic secondary metabolites of host plants (HammerandBowers2015). Since the 1980s, the detoxification of exogenous substances mediated by symbiotic microorganisms has been repeatedly proposed. Dowd and Shen conducted their first experiment and discovered that when the symbiotic yeast Symbiotaphrina kochii in tobacco tobacco Lasioderma serricorne was removed, It is more susceptible to phenolic plant toxins (flavonoids, resorcinol, tannic acid) (Dowd 1989, Dowd and Shen 2011).

Based on this, this paper takes the citrus fruit fly as the research object and explores through bioassays whether intestinal microorganisms play a role in combating phenolic toxic secondary metabolites. By analyzing metatranscriptomic data, the molecular mechanism of phenolic degradation mediated by intestinal microbiota in the larvae of the citrus fruit fly was clarified. At the same time, key functional bacteria related to the degradation of phenolic substances were screened out to clarify the important role that functional bacteria play in assisting the larvae of the citrus fruit fly to improve their adaptability to phenolic substances, as well as the colonization and quantification of functional bacteria in the citrus fruit fly. Finally, the correlation between intestinal bacteria and fruit metabolites of citrus fruit fly larvae that feed on fruits of different hosts was explored. The above results will clarify the mechanism by which symbiotic bacteria assist the larvae of the citrus fruit fly in adapting to plant secondary metabolites, providing a theoretical basis for the use of plant secondary metabolites or symbiotic bacteria to control pests.

# Candidates for chemosensory genes identified in the Chinese citrus fly, Bactrocera minax, through a transcriptomic analysis  
## Abstract  
Background: The males of many Bactrocera species (Diptera: Tephritidae) respond strongly to plant-derived chemicals (male lures) and can be divided into cue lure/raspberry ketone (CL/RK) responders, methyl eugenol (ME) responders and non-responders. Representing a non-responders, Bactrocera minax display unique olfactory sensory characteristics compared with other Bactrocera species. The chemical senses of insects mediate behaviors that are associated with survival and reproduction. Here, we report the generation of transcriptomes from antennae and the rectal glands of both male and female adults of B. minax using Illumina sequencing technology, and annotated gene families potentially responsible for chemosensory.

## Discussion  
In this study the microbiome associated with B. minax was identified and characterized by 454 FLX pyrosequencing. This study reports for the very first time the bacterial diversity and abundance associated with the immature stages of B. minax using a non-culture-based approach. A previous study on the bacterial community of this fruit fly focused only on the adult flies. The results from this study suggest that Enterobacteriaceae dominates all life stages of the fly. This family has also been reported to be dominant in other tephritids. In addition Klebsiella, Citrobacter, Enterobacter and Serratia have been reported as the dominant genera found in the gut and reproductive system of adult B. minax. The present study also reports similar findings.

Research has found that the intestinal microbiota of insects have a degrading effect on secondary metabolites of toxic plants (Hammer andBowers2015). However, due to the limitations of early research conditions, the truly functional symbiotic microbiota in the intestine have not been fully explored. It is even impossible to determine whether the inhibition or detoxification of plant-derived toxins by symbiotic microorganisms is due to the contribution of core microorganisms or the collaboration of the symbiotic microbial community. In recent years, based on research methods in physiology and molecular biology, combined with the latest sequencing technology, the detoxification symbiotic relationships among different insect groups, including Coleoptera, Diptera, Lepidoptera and hemiptera, have been revealed. The following lists several plant toxin detoxification mediated by insect intestinal symbiotic microorganisms that have been widely studied.  
2.1 Intestinal symbiotic microorganisms of pine pests mediate the detoxification of terpenes
2.2 The intestinal symbiotic microorganisms of coffee fruit borer mediate the detoxification of caffeine

From our results the OTUs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7 were shared by all life stages of the fly. This suggests the possibility of vertical transmission of these bacteria. Vertically transmitted bacteria in tephritids have been reported to be present in the larval stage and maintained throughout the adult stage. In addition, 4 of these core OTUs found in B. minax, were also present in the oriental fruit fly, suggesting that they may play key roles in the biology of the fly.

. It is speculated that symbiotic bacteria may mediate protein synthesis to provide the host with an adequate nitrogen source. In addition, among the pathways of exogenous substance biodegradation and metabolites, the expression level of Atrazinedegradation is the highest. Atrazine is a triazobenzene selective systemic and transmissible herbicide. It is speculated that intestinal microorganisms may also be involved in the degradation of certain pesticides. In subsequent experiments, it is possible to further explore the dominant functional bacteria that mediate the above-mentioned metabolic pathways and study the regulatory mechanisms in the "functional bacteria - host" interaction model.

## Conclusion  
This study reports for the very first time the symbiotic bacteria present in the gut of the different developmental stages of the Chinese citrus fly and compares this population with the microbiome present in the adult life stages. The results revealed that the gut of the Chinese citrus fly harbors a large diversity of microorganisms belonging to 8 different phyla. Though Proteobacteria phyla dominated in all life stages, there was a shift in the most abundant OTUs from early development to maturity. Core bacteria groups shared by all life stages and different fruit flies belonged to the Enterobacteriaceae and the Enterococcaceae families. These species have also been found in other fruit fly groups and some have been reported to play significant roles in the biology of other fruit flies. These could be important targets for the further research on how symbiotic bacteria could be exploited in the management of fruit flies.

In summary, we applied metatranscriptomic sequencing analysis, match of symbiotic bacteria with functional genes,  isolation and identification of symbiotic bacteria as well as functional verification in this study. Our results show  that S. marcescens and E. faecalis confer the larvae in degrading fruit phenolic compounds,  promoting the growth and development of larvae,  and enhancing their adaptability to host fruits. Both bacteria can stably colonize in the gut of larvae and adult. S.  marcescens and E. faecalis in the larvae contain key genes catechol 1,2 dioxygenase gene and catechol 2,3 dioxygenase gene that help degrade phenolic compounds. The results revealed the mechanism by which B. minax larvae degrade phenolic  compounds and improve host adaptability via gut symbionts. Meantime,  it provides new insights into the interaction between specialized insects and host plants mediated by symbionts.

Metatranscriptomic sequencing analysis results showed that the abundance and diversity of gut symbionts in adults were  higher than those in larvae and pupae. Fimicutes was the dominant phylum in the adults,  while Proteobacteria dominated in both the larvae and pupae. At the genus level, Lactococcus dominated in adults,  Providencia in larvae,  and Achromobacter in pupae. The functional annotation of larvae by KEGG showed that gut microbiota was mainly abundant  in carbon metabolism (32.89%), energy metabolism (20.49%) amino acid metabolism (14.21%) and nucleic acid metabolism (7.79%). In addition the larval gut microbiota was also involved in the xenobiotic degradation metabolism. Detailed annotation of the  xenobiotic degradation metabolism revealed that a large number of genes in larval gut microbiota were involved in  benzene and benzoate degradation. After constructing phenolic compounds degradation pathway,  we found the key genes catechol 1,2-dioxygenase (C12O) and catechol 2,3-dioxygenase (C23O) were related to the degradation of phenolic substances, whereas these two genes are absent in the genome of B. minax,  hinting that the degradation of phenols may be completed by gut symbionts. Through the matching of genes and bacteria,  we found that Serratia marcescens contains the gene encoding catechol 1,2-dioxygenase and Enterococcus faecalis contains the gene encoding catechol 2,3-dioxygenase. The above results showed that the gut symbionts of B. minax larvae mediated the degradation of phenolic compounds.

## Introduction  
The gut of most insects is colonized by microbial communities, which vary in diversity and function across the different insect groups. Gut microbial colonization is affected by the morphology and physiology of the gut. The origin of gut bacteria are from horizontal or vertical transmissions and some important bacteria groups have evolved to develop intimate relations with insects. In social insects such as the honey bee, social interaction often leads to the transfer of important gut bacteria. In other insect groups such as the tephritids, the diversity and transmission patterns of important bacteria groups are poorly understood.  
The gut of Tephritidae has been shown to be colonized by diverse symbiotic bacteria mainly belonging to the phylum Proteobacteria, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, Actinodetes and Tenericutes. In tephritids, associations with symbiotic bacteria was first reported about a century ago, though the role these microorganisms play in their relationship with fruit flies was first reported about half a century later. Over the years, many studies have focused on understanding the roles bacteria play in symbiotic relationships with tephritid flies. For example, Wolbachia was previously reported as an infective species manipulating the reproductive system of most insects, but has recently been shown to have a mutualistic relationship with the bed bug.

The citrus fruit fly Bactrocera minax belongs to the order Diptera and the family Bactroceridae. It is an obligate pest. The larvae only feed on and damage various fruits of the Rudeaceae family and citrus genus, such as navel oranges, tangerines, Pong tangerines, lemons, etc. It is an important pest on citrus fruit trees (Chen et al 2016). Female adult insects lay eggs in unripe citrus fruits. After the eggs hatch, the larvae feed on the pulp inside the citrus. Due to the egg-laying selection of female insects, the larvae must overcome the defense of secondary metabolites in immature citrus fruits to complete their growth and development. Unripe citrus fruits contain a large amount of phenolic compounds. Especially after being infected by the larvae of the citrus fruit fly, the contents of two phenolic substances, conifol and coumaraldehyde, in the fruits increase significantly (Zhang et al 2022b). Phenols can directly act as toxins for herbivorous insects or be oxidized into toxic metabolites by peroxidase or polyphenol oxidase. These metabolites can cause physiological disorders in the growth and development of insects. However, it remains unclear how the larvae of the citrus fruit fly utilize intestinal microorganisms to adapt to unripe citrus fruits and overcome the defense response against phenolic secondary metabolites

Insect guts are also important physiological tissues and are favorable for the colonization of microorganisms because of their attributes, such as simple access to nutrients and defense against diverse environmental stressors. The gut microbes are indispensable because they offer benefits to the host in multiple aspects, including detoxification of plant allelochemicals, provision of nutrition for host insects, and digestion of complex carbohydrates. Intestinal microorganisms are engaged in several life processes of host insects, such as maintaining intestinal homeostasis, increasing oviposition, fecundity, and longevity of the host, controlling the insect immune system to protect against injury from external organisms, and altering insect behavior. The microorganisms of D. citri have also recently received widespread attention. Five different species of endosymbiotic microbiota of D. citri, including the mycetocyte symbiont, the syncytium symbiont, Arsenophonus sp., Wolbachia sp., and Liberobacter sp., were discovered. Understanding the bacteria community structure in different fruit flies will be a first step towards realizing how the roles symbiotic bacteria plays could be exploited in developing an integrated pest management strategy for these flies.  
The Chinese citrus fly Bactrocera minax (Enderlein) is considered unique in the Tephritidae family because of its long over-wintering pupal diapause and its single host, the citrus. B. minax causes huge damage to citrus in China, Nepal, India and Bhutan where it is a major pest. Their overwintering capability with six months of long diapause makes it difficult to manage this pest. So far chemical control has shown to be ineffective probably due to the presence of Gluthinone S-tranferase which plays an important role in detoxification of several insecticides contributing to insecticide resistance in this pest. In addition, commercially available pheromone attractive lures for B. minax males are unavailable. Therefore, there is an urgent need to seek alternative control strategies for their management.

In fact, insects are multiorganismal symbionts and harbor many microbes that also mediate insecticide resistance (Douglas, 2015). ## Abstract  
Background: Symbiotic bacteria play a critical role in insect's biology. They also offer great opportunities to improve on current pest management techniques. In order to exploit and integrate the roles played by the gut microbiota on pest management programs, a better understanding of the structural organization of the microbial community in the Chinese citrus fly Bactrocera minax is essential.  
Results: The results revealed a total of 162 OTUs at 97% similarity interval. The dominant bacteria phyla were Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Antinobacteria and Firmicutes, with the Proteobacteria having the highest relative abundance (more than 80% in all life stages). There was also a shift in the dominant OTUs from the early developmental stages to the late developmental stages and adult stages in B. minax. These OTUs related to Klebsiella pneumoniae, Providencia rettgeri and Enterobacter aerogenes, respectively. Six bacteria OTU were shared by all the life stages. These belonged to the Enterobacteriaceae and the Enterococcaceae families.  
Conclusion: The common bacteria groups shared by all the life stages and other fruit flies could be important targets for further research. This should aim towards realizing how these bacteria affect the biology of the fly and how their relationship could be exploited in the development of sustainable management strategies against fruit flies.

Recent evidence suggests that the interaction between herbivorous insects and their host plants is mediated by the gut microbiome, which refers to all the microorganisms (i.e., bacteria, fungi, viruses, archaea) that reside within the gut. Studies have linked the gut microbiome to key insect physiological and biological functions, including energy provision, nutrient uptake, growth, degradation of plant toxins and pesticides, and shaping of the immune system (reviewed in 15, 16). These insect-microbiota interactions can influence plant-insect relationships both directly and indirectly. For example, certain gut bacteria mediate host plant selection by influencing insect preferences and aiding in the identification of sui for feeding and reproduction. Once on the plant, insects encounter challenges such as low nutritional quality, indigestible plant tissues, and toxic secondary metabolites. Gut bacteria help overcome these obstacles by enhancing digestion, supplying essential nutrients, and detoxifying harmful compounds, allowing insects to exploit otherwise unsui. Conversely, plant defenses or poor-quality plant tissue can disrupt the gut microbiota (dysbiosis), and may negatively impact insect health, development, and survival [reviewed in (17)].

Different members of these Enterobacteriaceae group have been shown to play different fitness roles in fruit flies. In B. oleae for example symbiotic bacteria Candidatus Erwinia dacicola helps the young larvae to overcome host defence. The most dominant OTUs in the egg, first and second instar larva were related to Klebsiella pneumoniae LC216325.1. Klebsiella spp has been isolated from the gut of other tephritids.  
Bacteria belonging to this genus could act as an attractive lure for fruit flies and improve on mating competitiveness in fruit flies. It has also been shown to have nitrogen fixing properties.  
The dominant OTU in the pupae is related to P. rettgeri. Similar member belonging to this genus has been identified in different tephritids. B. minax undergoes diapause during harsh winter. The high relative abundance of Providencia in third instar larvae and pupae, but not other life stages, suggests that it might be playing a role in diapause. A shift in gut bacteria community structure has been reported in diapausing insects and obese humans who have large fat reserves. Providencia has been shown to have nitrifying-denitrifying functions, thereby converting ammonia into less toxic waste. Speculatively Providencia present in the BM3L and BMP are likely to help the insect remove metabolic waste during the long diapause period. However, more research needs to be carried out to confirm this hypothesis.

In this study the microbiome associated with B. minax was identified and characterized by 454 FLX pyrosequencing. This study reports for the very first time the bacterial diversity and abundance associated with the immature stages of B. minax using a non-culture-based approach. A previous study on the bacterial community of this fruit fly focused only on the adult flies. The results from this study suggest that Enterobacteriaceae dominates all life stages of the fly. This family has also been reported to be dominant in other tephritids. Insects harbor diverse bacterial communities, which have profound effects on the host. These symbionts can range from disease-causing to commensal and mutually beneficial microbes. ## Conclusion  
This study reports for the very first time the symbiotic bacteria present in the gut of the different developmental stages of the Chinese citrus fly and compares this population with the microbiome present in the adult life stages. The results revealed that the gut of the Chinese citrus fly harbors a large diversity of microorganisms belonging to 8 different phyla. Though Proteobacteria phyla dominated in all life stages, there was a shift in the most abundant OTUs from early development to maturity. Core bacteria groups shared by all life stages and different fruit flies belonged to the Enterobacteriaceae and the Enterococcaceae families. These species have also been found in other fruit fly groups and some have been reported to play significant roles in the biology of other fruit flies. These could be important targets for the further research on how symbiotic bacteria could be exploited in the management of fruit flies.

## Introduction  
The gut of most insects is colonized by microbial communities, which vary in diversity and function across the different insect groups. Gut microbial colonization is affected by the morphology and physiology of the gut. The origin of gut bacteria are from horizontal or vertical transmissions and some important bacteria groups have evolved to develop intimate relations with insects. In social insects such as the honey bee, social interaction often leads to the transfer of important gut bacteria. In other insect groups such as the tephritids, the diversity and transmission patterns of important bacteria groups are poorly understood.

Over the years, many studies have focused on understanding the roles bacteria play in symbiotic relationships with tephritid flies. Symbiotic microorganisms usually exhibit strict host tissue orientation and are located in symbiotic organs, and due to the diversity of insect species, the localization patterns also show diversity (Moranet al 1998). In contrast, most detoxifying symbiotic microorganisms are what is called "intestinal symbiosis". The intestines of insects are usually divided into three areas: the foregut, the midgut and the hindgut. The midgut is the site where insects digest food and is also the main intestinal area for detoxification and metabolic processes. For instance, Megacopta cribraria and Riptortus pedestris formed many sac-like tissues in the posterior midgut region, which were filled with symbiotic bacteria (Kikuchiet al 2005). ## Conclusions  
The current investigation is the first study into acaricidal properties of three bacterial species isolated from unexploited ecosystems against citrus rust mite. The current study showed that S. thinghirensis strain HM3 and S. tricolor strain HM10 are efficient in controlling citrus rust mite, P. oleivora populations under field and lab conditions, whereas B. subtilis produces moderate control. Therefore, pathogenic bacteria can be used as a potential microbial control on P. oleivora in a program of integrated pest management (IPM) to control P. oleivora in the orange orchards, offering a viable alternative to conventional synthetic acaricides. Nevertheless, besides their ability to kill mite and inhibitory effects on the eggs hatching in the present study, the variety of bioactive substances produced by Streptomyces spp. includes substances capable of enhancing plant growth. Moreover, complementary research should be conducted to evaluate the potential of these bacterial species in mite pests' management programs in orchards as an approach to meeting the increasing demand for nonchemical control strategies.

## Detoxification  
Glutathione-s-transferases (GST) are a family of detoxification enzymes found in insects and almost all animals. GSTs detoxify exogenous compounds, including plant and microbial toxins, and pesticides (Kostaropoulos et al., 2001; Ortelli et al., 2003). In addition to detoxification, GSTs function in response to oxidative stress. Reactive oxygen compounds produced in response to microbial challenge are also cytotoxic to host tissues (Ranson and Hemingway, 2005). Insect GSTs were originally classified into type-1 and type-2, but further studies have broken these into delta, epsilon, omega, theta, and zeta groups (Ranson and Hemingway, 2005).  
Ten GSTs were identified in D. citri. In a phylogenetic comparison to identify GST group, two sequences aligned with microsomal, two with epsilon, two with delta, and three with sigma type GSTs. One D. citri GST did not align to any classified GSTs used in the analysis. No D. citri GSTs showed similarity to zeta, omega, or theta types. Kumar et al. (2003) reported that impaired GST function in a strain of A. gambiae reduced their ability to acquire Plasmodium parasites due to the oxidative stress inducing conditions favorable to melanin encapsulation. In D. citri, induction of high oxidative stress may inhibit acquisition of CLas, thus GSTs could be a target for future research to prevent or reduce CLas transmission. Further investigations will determine the role of these GST genes in D. citri immune function and pesticide detoxification.

In fact, insects are multiorganismal symbionts and harbor many microbes that also mediate insecticide resistance (Douglas, 2015). An early study found that Pseudomonas melophthora, an obligate symbiont, helped an insect host (apple maggot, Rhagoletis pomonella) degrade 6 insecticides (Boush and Matsumura, 1967). The densities of symbiotic bacteria Arsenophonus, Rickettsia, and Wolbachia from the Q biotype whitefly associated with the host's susceptibility to thiamethoxam, imidacloprid, pyriproxyfen, and spiromesifen (Ghanim and Kontsedalov, 2009). (2018) found that Arsenophonus strains (S-type Arsenophonus) in the BPH negatively affected the insecticide resistance of the host by downregulating xenobiotic metabolism and increasing amino acid accumulation.

Insect guts are also important physiological tissues and are favorable for the colonization of microorganisms because of their attributes, such as simple access to nutrients and defense against diverse environmental stressors. The gut microbes are indispensable because they offer benefits to the host in multiple aspects, including detoxification of plant allelochemicals, provision of nutrition for host insects, and digestion of complex carbohydrates. Intestinal microorganisms are engaged in several life processes of host insects, such as maintaining intestinal homeostasis, increasing oviposition, fecundity, and longevity of the host, controlling the insect immune system to protect against injury from external organisms, and altering insect behavior. The microorganisms of D. citri have also recently received widespread attention. Five different species of endosymbiotic microbiota of D. citri, including the mycetocyte symbiont, the syncytium symbiont, Arsenophonus sp., Wolbachia sp., and Liberobacter sp., were discovered. The microbial diversity of D. citri was also studied by restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) and denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE) analyses of 16 S rDNA sequences, and the results showed that the syncytium endosymbiont is a dominant bacterial flora.

The detoxification metabolism of insect intestinal microorganisms and their hosts  
During the interaction between herbivorous insects and plants, in order to better adapt to various toxic secondary metabolites produced by plants, various counter-defense strategies have also evolved (Pentzoldet al 2014). The counter-defense strategies of herbivorous insects are complex and diverse (Mckenzie et al 2002, Dong et al 2020, Liu et al 2021). The digestive enzyme system of herbivorous insects is an important component of their defense against plants and plays a significant detoxification role. For instance, the nitrile-specific protein in the intestine of Pieris rapae, the cabbage powder, specifically mediates the hydrolysis reaction of glucosinolates - myrosinase to produce nitriles instead of toxic isothiocyanates (Wittstock et al 2004). The detoxification enzymes in insects, such as the cytochrome P450 enzyme system, are an important way to mediate the development of resistance by herbivorous insects to host plants. For example, CYP6B1-8 and CYP321A1 of lepidoptera insects have high metabolic activity against furanocoumarins, etc. (Chunget al 2007); CYP6CM1 and CYP6CY3 in Myzus persicae, CYP6CY3 in Drosophilamelanogaster, and CYP6B1 and CYP6B3 in Papilio polyxenes It can mediate nicotine metabolism (Puinean et al 2010, Macel 2011, Silva et al 2012). The citrus fruit fly Bactrocera minax belongs to the order Diptera and the family Bactroceridae. It is an obligate pest. The larvae only feed on and damage various fruits of the Rudeaceae family and citrus genus, such as navel oranges, tangerines, Pong tangerines, lemons, etc. It is an important pest on citrus fruit trees (Chen et al 2016). Female adult insects lay eggs in unripe citrus fruits. After the eggs hatch, the larvae feed on the pulp inside the citrus. Due to the egg-laying selection of female insects, the larvae must overcome the defense of secondary metabolites in immature citrus fruits to complete their growth and development. Unripe citrus fruits contain a large amount of phenolic compounds. Especially after being infected by the larvae of the citrus fruit fly, the contents of two phenolic substances, conifol and coumaraldehyde, in the fruits increase significantly (Zhang et al 2022b). Phenols can directly act as toxins for herbivorous insects or be oxidized into toxic metabolites by peroxidase or polyphenol oxidase. These metabolites can cause physiological disorders in the growth and development of insects. However, it remains unclear how the larvae of the citrus fruit fly utilize intestinal microorganisms to adapt to unripe citrus fruits and overcome the defense response against phenolic secondary metabolites

Recent evidence suggests that the interaction between herbivorous insects and their host plants is mediated by the gut microbiome, which refers to all the microorganisms (i.e., bacteria, fungi, viruses, archaea) that reside within the gut. Studies have linked the gut microbiome to key insect physiological and biological functions, including energy provision, nutrient uptake, growth, degradation of plant toxins and pesticides, and shaping of the immune system (reviewed in 15, 16). These insect-microbiota interactions can influence plant-insect relationships both directly and indirectly. For example, certain gut bacteria mediate host plant selection by influencing insect preferences and aiding in the identification of sui for feeding and reproduction. Once on the plant, insects encounter challenges such as low nutritional quality, indigestible plant tissues, and toxic secondary metabolites. Gut bacteria help overcome these obstacles by enhancing digestion, supplying essential nutrients, and detoxifying harmful compounds, allowing insects to exploit otherwise unsui. Conversely, plant defenses or poor-quality plant tissue can disrupt the gut microbiota (dysbiosis), and may negatively impact insect health, development, and survival [reviewed in (17)].

Results: The results revealed a total of 162 OTUs at 97% similarity interval. The Chinese citrus fly Bactrocera minax (Enderlein) is considered unique in the Tephritidae family because of its long over-wintering pupal diapause and its single host, the citrus. B. minax causes huge damage to citrus in China, Nepal, India and Bhutan where it is a major pest. Their overwintering capability with six months of long diapause makes it difficult to manage this pest. ## Conclusion  
This study reports for the very first time the symbiotic bacteria present in the gut of the different developmental stages of the Chinese citrus fly and compares this population with the microbiome present in the adult life stages. The results revealed that the gut of the Chinese citrus fly harbors a large diversity of microorganisms belonging to 8 different phyla. Though Proteobacteria phyla dominated in all life stages, there was a shift in the most abundant OTUs from early development to maturity. Core bacteria groups shared by all life stages and different fruit flies belonged to the Enterobacteriaceae and the Enterococcaceae families. These species have also been found in other fruit fly groups and some have been reported to play significant roles in the biology of other fruit flies. These could be important targets for the further research on how symbiotic bacteria could be exploited in the management of fruit flies.

## Introduction  
The gut of most insects is colonized by microbial communities, which vary in diversity and function across the different insect groups. Gut microbial colonization is affected by the morphology and physiology of the gut. The origin of gut bacteria are from horizontal or vertical transmissions and some important bacteria groups have evolved to develop intimate relations with insects. In social insects such as the honey bee, social interaction often leads to the transfer of important gut bacteria. In other insect groups such as the tephritids, the diversity and transmission patterns of important bacteria groups are poorly understood.  
The gut of Tephritidae has been shown to be colonized by diverse symbiotic bacteria mainly belonging to the phylum Proteobacteria, Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes, Actinodetes and Tenericutes. In tephritids, associations with symbiotic bacteria was first reported about a century ago, though the role these microorganisms play in their relationship with fruit flies was first reported about half a century later. Over the years, many studies have focused on understanding the roles bacteria play in symbiotic relationships with tephritid flies. For example, Wolbachia was previously reported as an infective species manipulating the reproductive system of most insects, but has recently been shown to have a mutualistic relationship with the bed bug.

Recent evidence suggests that the interaction between herbivorous insects and their host plants is mediated by the gut microbiome, which refers to all the microorganisms (i.e., bacteria, fungi, viruses, archaea) that reside within the gut. Studies have linked the gut microbiome to key insect physiological and biological functions, including energy provision, nutrient uptake, growth, degradation of plant toxins and pesticides, and shaping of the immune system (reviewed in 15, 16). These insect-microbiota interactions can influence plant-insect relationships both directly and indirectly. For example, certain gut bacteria mediate host plant selection by influencing insect preferences and aiding in the identification of sui for feeding and reproduction. Once on the plant, insects encounter challenges such as low nutritional quality, indigestible plant tissues, and toxic secondary metabolites. Gut bacteria help overcome these obstacles by enhancing digestion, supplying essential nutrients, and detoxifying harmful compounds, allowing insects to exploit otherwise unsui. Conversely, plant defenses or poor-quality plant tissue can disrupt the gut microbiota (dysbiosis), and may negatively impact insect health, development, and survival [reviewed in (17)].

Insects harbor diverse bacterial communities, which have profound effects on the host. These symbionts can range from disease-causing to commensal and mutually beneficial microbes. Because of their associations with symbionts, insects, in particular, are accelerating their evolutionary and ecological diversification. Microbial symbionts are also involved in the biology of insect hosts, such as the detoxification of compounds (Kikuchi et al., 2012; Ceja-Navarro et al., 2015), defense against natural enemies (Fieck et al., 2010), promotion of heat tolerance (Engel and Moran, 2013), mediating intra- and interspecific communication (Wada-Katsumata et al., 2015), and providing nutrition to the host insect. For example, aphids feed on plant sap and rely on an endosymbiotic bacterium, Buchnera aphidicola, to produce essential amino acids that are limited in plant phloem (Douglas, 1998). Rhodococcus spp. in triatomine bugs contributes to the insect's metabolism by synthesizing B-complex vitamins that are deficient in a blood diet (Beard et al., 2002; Moran et al., 2003). Alternatively, microbial symbionts could involve the host in transmitting pathogens (Kambris et al., 2009; Hancock et al., 2011).

In summary, we applied metatranscriptomic sequencing analysis, match of symbiotic bacteria with functional genes,  isolation and identification of symbiotic bacteria as well as functional verification in this study. Our results show  that S. marcescens and E. faecalis confer the larvae in degrading fruit phenolic compounds,  promoting the growth and development of larvae,  and enhancing their adaptability to host fruits. Both bacteria can stably colonize in the gut of larvae and adult. S.  marcescens and E. faecalis in the larvae contain key genes catechol 1,2 dioxygenase gene and catechol 2,3 dioxygenase gene that help degrade phenolic compounds. The results revealed the mechanism by which B. minax larvae degrade phenolic  compounds and improve host adaptability via gut symbionts. Meantime,  it provides new insights into the interaction between specialized insects and host plants mediated by symbionts.

## CONCLUSIONS  
Our study provides the transcriptional evidences hinting at a multiple metabolic mechanism involved in the development of fenpropathrin resistance in the field population of P. citri. In order to understand comprehensively the underlying mechanisms conferring fenpropathrin resistance, those upregulated resistance-associated transcripts identified in resistant mites would be considered as the key candidate target genes for further function analysis. Alternatively, GSTs play an antioxidant role in alleviating the oxidative stress caused by fenpropathrin. Recent evidence suggests that the interaction between herbivorous insects and their host plants is mediated by the gut microbiome, which refers to all the microorganisms (i.e., bacteria, fungi, viruses, archaea) that reside within the gut. Studies have linked the gut microbiome to key insect physiological and biological functions, including energy provision, nutrient uptake, growth, degradation of plant toxins and pesticides, and shaping of the immune system (reviewed in 15, 16). These insect-microbiota interactions can influence plant-insect relationships both directly and indirectly. For example, certain gut bacteria mediate host plant selection by influencing insect preferences and aiding in the identification of sui for feeding and reproduction. Once on the plant, insects encounter challenges such as low nutritional quality, indigestible plant tissues, and toxic secondary metabolites. Gut bacteria help overcome these obstacles by enhancing digestion, supplying essential nutrients, and detoxifying harmful compounds, allowing insects to exploit otherwise unsui. Conversely, plant defenses or poor-quality plant tissue can disrupt the gut microbiota (dysbiosis), and may negatively impact insect health, development, and survival [reviewed in (17)].

Studies have linked the gut microbiome to key insect physiological and biological functions, including energy provision, nutrient uptake, growth, degradation of plant toxins and pesticides, and shaping of the immune system (reviewed in 15, 16). These insect-microbiota interactions can influence plant-insect relationships both directly and indirectly. For example, certain gut bacteria mediate host plant selection by influencing insect preferences and aiding in the identification of sui for feeding and reproduction. Once on the plant, insects encounter challenges such as low nutritional quality, indigestible plant tissues, and toxic secondary metabolites. Gut bacteria help overcome these obstacles by enhancing digestion, supplying essential nutrients, and detoxifying harmful compounds, allowing insects to exploit otherwise unsui. Conversely, plant defenses or poor-quality plant tissue can disrupt the gut microbiota (dysbiosis), and may negatively impact insect health, development, and survival [reviewed in (17)].

The symbiotic bacteria in insects attach to the intestinal surface, forming a biofilm (Beer and Stoodley 2006). The formation of biofilms is conducive to the specific functions of symbiotic bacteria (Marques et al 2002, Maltz et al 2012). The symbiotic bacteria in the biofilm have a degradation effect on toxic substances in food, thereby alleviating the damage caused by toxic substances to the insect intestine. For example, Acinetobacter colonized in the intestine of the Lymantria dispar moth can degrade toxic glycosides (Mason et al 2014).

A citrus peel contains pectin, a natural gelling agent commonly utilized in jams, jellies, dairy products, desserts, soft drinks, frozen foods, and pharmaceuticals. Pectin, a naturally occurring polymer in higher plants, can be classified into three main groups based on distinct characteristics. The first group, homogalacturonan (HG), is known as the “smooth region” due to its linear structure consisting of alpha -(1,4)-linked galacturonic acid. The second group, rhamnogalacturonan-I (RG-I), referred to as the “hair region”, is primarily branched and accounts for 20–30% of the pectin domain. The third group, RG-II, makes up approximately 10% of the total pectin domain and is the most complex group, containing 12 different monosaccharides and over 20 types of linkages. RG-II is characterized by substituted galacturonans (GS) and is considered the most intricate segment of pectin. Pectin can be classified based on its degree of esterification, which refers to the ratio of esterified carboxylic acid units to the total carboxylic acid units in the pectin structure. There are two main types, namely low-methoxyl (LM) pectin, with fewer than 50% esterified carboxyl groups, and high-methoxyl (HM) pectin, with more than 50% esterified carboxyl groups. The degree of esterification is crucial as it directly impacts pectin’s structure and functional properties.
